title: OpenClaw for Marketing and Content Teams: 6 Workflows That Run 24/7
summary: OpenClaw for marketing content teams: 6 automation workflows for research, drafting, and publishing. Content agents running 24/7 — not just when your laptop is on.
body_text: Workflow 2: Competitive intelligence digest What it does: Every Monday at 7am, OpenClaw checks your competitor blogs, identifies new articles published in the last 7 days, summarizes each one with key takeaways and gaps, and sends a digest to the team in Slack. Skills used: fetch_url , rss_feed_reader , summarize_content , send_slack_message Setup time: 1–2 hours to configure competitor URLs and digest format How it works: OpenClaw has a configured list of competitor blog RSS feeds (you provide these once) Every Monday morning, it fetches and reads all new articles published since the last run For each article, it extracts: the main argument, key statistics cited, what angle they're taking, and what they didn't cover The digest arrives in Slack formatted as a scannable list: "3 new articles from [Competitor]. [Article 1 summary]. [Gap: they didn't address X]." What humans still do: Strategic decisions — which gaps to pursue, which angles to counter, which topics aren't worth addressing. This is the workflow teams describe as having the biggest ROI. Competitive monitoring that used to take 2–3 hours per week takes 20 minutes of review time instead. Workflow 3: SEO brief generation What it does: Given a target keyword, OpenClaw researches the top-ranking articles, analyzes what they cover and what they miss, and generates a structured content brief with recommended headings, key points to cover, statistics to cite, and gaps to fill. Skills used: web_search , fetch_url , analyze_content , write_brief Setup time: 30–45 minutes to configure your brief template format How it works: You (or a teammate) send OpenClaw a keyword via Slack: "@openclaw brief: best restaurant booking apps" OpenClaw searches Google for the keyword, fetches and reads the top 5–8 organic results It identifies: which sections appear in most results (table stakes), which sections appear in only 1–2 results (differentiation opportunities), what statistics are cited, what questions remain unanswered It outputs a structured brief in your Google Docs folder: recommended H2s, key points per section, statistics sources, and a "differentiation angle" based on the gaps it found What humans still do: Validate the brief, add firsthand expertise, identify which differentiating angles align with your strategy. Workflow 4: Social media repurposing What it does: When an article is published (detected via RSS or webhook), OpenClaw reads the full article and generates 5 Twitter/X thread drafts, 3 LinkedIn post drafts, and a newsletter excerpt — all in separate Slack threads for quick review and approval. Skills used: rss_feed_reader or webhook trigger, fetch_url , reformat_for_social , send_slack_message Setup time: 1–2 hours to configure tone guidelines and social format templates per channel How it works: OpenClaw monitors your blog's RSS feed for new publications Within 15 minutes of a new article appearing, it reads the full content It generates: Twitter threads (hook + 4-6 tweet thread for each of 5 different angles), LinkedIn posts (more formal, insight-focused), newsletter excerpt (200-word summary with the key takeaway) Each format arrives in a dedicated Slack channel ( #social-drafts ) as a separate thread What humans still do: Pick the best angle from the 5 Twitter options, lightly edit the LinkedIn copy for voice consistency, hit post. What used to take 45 minutes per article takes 5–10 minutes. Teams report that having 5 Twitter thread options rather than 1 leads to significantly better engagement — OpenClaw generates variety, humans pick the winner. The "just edit one draft" model produces more uniform output than "choose from several angles." Workflow 5: Brand mention and sentiment monitoring What it does: OpenClaw checks Reddit, Hacker News, and Twitter/X daily for brand mentions, summarizes sentiment and specific criticisms or praise, and flags anything requiring a response within 4 hours. Skills used: search_reddit , search_hackernews , web_search , analyze_sentiment , send_slack_message Setup time: 45–60 minutes to configure brand terms and urgency escalation rules How it works: Every 6 hours, OpenClaw searches for your brand name, product name, and key variants across Reddit and Hacker News It reads each mention thread and classifies it: positive, neutral, negative, or requires-response It sends a daily digest summarizing total mentions, sentiment breakdown, and notable threads It immediately flags threads marked as "requires-response" (criticism with traction, false information spreading, support questions going unanswered) to a dedicated #brand-alerts Slack channel What humans still do: Decide whether and how to respond. OpenClaw identifies the situation and surfaces it; your team makes the call. No agent should post a response on your brand's behalf without human approval. Workflow 6: Weekly newsletter compilation What it does: Every Friday at 2pm, OpenClaw compiles the week's published articles, social posts, and notable industry news into a formatted newsletter draft — ready for final review and send. Skills used: rss_feed_reader , fetch_url , web_search , compile_newsletter , write_to_google_docs Setup time: 2–3 hours to set up newsletter template and curation criteria How it works: OpenClaw pulls everything published to your blog that week It summarizes each article in 1–2 sentences with the key takeaway It pulls 2–3 relevant industry news items from configured RSS sources (curated in advance — you control which feeds it watches) It formats the full newsletter in your template in Google Docs, with a draft subject line and preview text By 3pm Friday, the newsletter is in your inbox ready for a 15-minute review and send What humans still do: Review the curation choices, adjust the subject line, add any personal notes from the editor. The compilation, formatting, and linking all happen without manual effort. What still needs humans OpenClaw is remarkably capable. It also has real limitations. Always keep humans in the loop for: Final editorial voice — OpenClaw writes well, but consistent brand voice requires human review. Every draft that goes to publication should have a human pass. Original interviews and firsthand reporting — OpenClaw can't call a source. Any content requiring original interviews, expert quotes from real people, or firsthand observation needs human legwork. Strategic decisions — which topics to pursue, which competitor angles to counter, what your editorial positioning should be. These are judgment calls based on context OpenClaw doesn't have. Legal and compliance review — anything touching regulated industries, legal claims, or sensitive topics needs a human check. OpenClaw is not a lawyer. Crisis communications — when something goes wrong and the brand response matters, humans need to write and approve every word. The teams that get the most value from OpenClaw treat it as a capable junior researcher and production assistant — not as a replacement for editorial judgment. Getting started with content automation The fastest way to start: pick Workflow 2 (competitive intelligence digest) and run it for two weeks. It's the lowest-risk workflow — OpenClaw reads competitor articles, you review the summary. Nothing goes public without your approval. Once you've seen how it works and calibrated the output quality, add Workflow 4 (social repurposing) and Workflow 6 (newsletter compilation). Those two together cover the highest-volume repetitive work most content teams face. No Docker needed, no VPS setup — Blink Claw runs your content agent 24/7 for $22/mo all-in, with 200+ LLM models included. Your Monday morning digest arrives whether you're at your desk or at the airport. Frequently Asked Questions OpenClaw doesn't post publicly by default — it drafts to Slack or Google Docs for human review. You configure which actions require approval (all of them, initially) and which can run autonomously. Most content teams keep all public-facing outputs gated behind human review indefinitely. The efficiency gain is in research and drafting, not in autonomous publishing. OpenClaw's skills include connectors for Notion, Airtable, Google Docs, Google Sheets, WordPress, and Webflow. For calendars and project tracking, Notion and Airtable are the most commonly used. For draft delivery, Google Docs gives editors the most familiar review experience. The 6 workflows described here take 10–15 hours total to configure correctly — roughly 1–3 hours each. The highest setup investment is the content calendar automation (Workflow 1) because you need to define the brief template and test quality output before trusting it with real topics. Competitive monitoring (Workflow 2) is the fastest to get running, typically under 2 hours. It can approximate your brand voice if you give it examples. Include 3–5 representative articles in the agent configuration as style references. OpenClaw will pattern-match tone, sentence length, and word choice. You'll still need to review and edit for voice consistency, but the gap between first draft and final is smaller when style references are provided. Zapier connects pre-built triggers to pre-built actions. OpenClaw can reason about content. Zapier can "when a new RSS item appears, send it to Slack." OpenClaw can "when a new competitor article appears, read it, identify the key argument and gaps, and send an editorial commentary to Slack." The reasoning layer is what makes content-specific automation genuinely useful rather than just mechanical data transfer. Blink Claw hosts OpenClaw 24/7 so the reasoning runs continuously, not just when your team is at their desks.

title: authID Reports Financial and Operating Results for the First Quarter 2026
summary: DENVER, May 14, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- authID® (Nasdaq: AUID) (“authID” or the “Company”), a leading provider of biometric identity verification and authentication solutions, today reported financial and operating results for the Quarter ended March 31, 2026. F irst Quarter 2026 vs.
body_text: PDF Version DENVER, May 14, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- authID® (Nasdaq: AUID) (“authID” or the “Company”), a leading provider of biometric identity verification and authentication solutions, today reported financial and operating results for the Quarter ended March 31, 2026. F irst Quarter 2026 vs. First Quarter 2025 Financial Summary Total revenue for the quarter was $0.5 million, compared to $0.3 million a year ago. Operating expenses were $5.0 million, compared to $4.7 million a year ago. Net loss was $4.5 million, or $0.28 per share, compared to a loss of $4.4 million, or $0.40 per share a year ago. Adjusted EBITDA Loss of $3.4 million (non-GAAP measure as defined below), compared with $3.9 million a year ago. Gross bARR (Booked Annual Recurring Revenue) of $0.08 million (non-GAAP measure as defined below), compared with $0.01 million a year ago. "Q1 2026 represents an inflection point for authID, as the Company executed a deliberate and multi-dimensional strategy, simultaneously strengthening the balance sheet, restructuring the cost base, advancing its technology leadership, and deepening its enterprise pipeline,” said Rhon Daguro authID CEO. “We took action to reduce our cost structure and secure our runway, in closing $4.2 million in bridge financing after the quarter closed. We expanded our channel presence through new partnerships in the Microsoft ecosystem and our enterprise POC pipeline continues to progress with some of the largest organizations in the world" added Daguro. “The combination of accelerating revenue, structural cost savings, and an expanding enterprise pipeline creates the conditions for authID to reach cash flow sustainability and long-term financial independence.” Recent Business and Operational Highlights The Company has built a $40m pipeline represented by 20 major accounts, with a growing number of accounts coming from our channel partner program. We are in various phases of Proofs of Concept with more than a dozen of these prospective major enterprise customers spanning retail, banking, fintech, crypto, industrial and chip manufacturing, and healthcare. Launched what the Company believes is the only biometric identity platform purpose-built to withstand quantum-era threats. authID's PrivacyKey™ platform now incorporates quantum-resistant cryptography, using NIST-standard quantum-resistant encryption algorithms and cryptographic key sharding, which eliminates single-point-of-failure vulnerabilities. Expanded our strategic partnership program adding Formula5, a Microsoft-focused consultancy specializing in identity, security, and Zero Trust architecture, to serve as a reseller and implementation partner for authID's biometric identity platform. Formula 5, like our existing partner MajorKey, operates within the security framework of Microsoft Entra and Microsoft Verified ID ecosystems — expanding the Company's reach into a broad range of industries including financial services, healthcare, energy and manufacturing. Secured $4.2 million in bridge financing subsequent to quarter end, extending the Company's operating runway as it continues to advance enterprise proof-of-concept evaluations and work towards closing significant deals. Financial Results for the First Quarter Ended March 31, 2026 Revenue for the three months ended March 31, 2026 was $0.5 million, compared with $0.3 million a year ago. Operating expenses for the three months ended March 31, 2026, were $5.0 million, compared to $4.7 million a year ago. The 2026 was driven by an increase of in stock-based compensation for employees and advisors, partially offset by employee and vendor expense reductions. Net loss for the three months ended March 31, 2026 was $4.5 million, of which non-cash charges were $1.1 million, compared with a net loss of $4.4 million a year ago, of which non-cash charges were $0.5 million. Loss per share for the three months ended March 31, 2026 was $0.28, compared with $0.40 a year ago. Adjusted EBITDA loss (a non-GAAP measure, as defined below) was $3.4 million for the three months ended March 31, 2026, compared with a loss of $3.9 million a year ago. The decrease in adjusted EBITDA loss is primarily driven by the decrease in operating expenses, net of non-cash stock-based compensation. Please refer to Table 1 for reconciliation of net loss to adjusted EBITDA (a non-GAAP measure). Remaining Performance Obligation (RPO) as of March 31, 2026, the Company’s Remaining Performance Obligation (RPO) was $2.0 million, of which $0.38 million is recorded as deferred revenue and $1.62 million is related to other non-cancellable contracted amounts. The Company expects approximately 71% of the RPO to be recognized as revenue over the twelve months ending March 31, 2027, based on contractual commitments and expected usage patterns. The gross amount of Booked Annual Recurring Revenue or bARR, (a non-GAAP measure, as defined below), signed in the first quarter of 2026 was $0.08 million, up from $0.01 million of gross bARR a year ago. The net amount of bARR was $0.08 million, compared to a negative $0.13 million of net bARR signed in the comparable period in 2025. The Q1 bARR is comprised of $0.03 million in Committed Annual Recurring Revenue (cARR) and $0.06 million in estimated Usage Above Commitments (UAC). The net amount of bARR reflects the deduction of the bARR of contracts previously included in reported bARR, due to certain customers experiencing delays in Production Go-Live timing, volume ramping and challenges meeting their contractual obligations. The amount of Annual Recurring Revenue or ARR, (a non-GAAP measure, as defined below) as of Q1 2026 was $1.9 million, compared to $1.2 million of ARR as of Q1 2025. See below for further definition and explanation of ARR and bARR, non-GAAP measures. Conference Call A conference call and webcast will be held today at 5:00p.m. EDT, hosted by authID Chief Executive Officer Rhon Daguro and Chief Financial Officer Ed Sellitto to discuss the financial results and provide a corporate update. To participate on the live conference call, please access this registration link and you will be provided with dial-in details. To avoid delays, participants are encouraged to dial into the conference call 15 minutes ahead of the scheduled start time. A live webcast of the call will also be available here and on the “Events & Presentations” page of the Company’s website at investors.authid.ai . Only participants on the live conference call will be able to ask questions. A replay of the event will also be available for 90 days at authID’s Investor Relations site. About authID Inc. authID® (Nasdaq: AUID) ensures enterprises “Know Who's Behind the Device™” for every customer or employee login and transaction through its easy-to-integrate, patented, biometric identity platform. authID quickly and accurately verifies a user's identity, leveraging a 1-in-1-billion False Positive Rate for the highest level of assurance, coupled with industry-leading speed and privacy-preserving technology. authID's IDX platform secures the distributed workforce of employees and contractors, while enforcing authorization and accountability for AI agents. By creating a biometric root of trust for each user, authID stops fraud at onboarding, prevents account takeover, detects and stops deepfakes, eliminates password risks and costs, and provides the fastest, frictionless, and most accurate user identity experience in the industry. Actual results may vary materially from the results anticipated by these forward-looking statements as a result of a variety of risk factors, including the Company’s ability to attract and retain customers; successful implementation of the services to be provided under new customer contracts and their adoption by customers’ users; the Company’s ability to compete effectively; changes in laws, regulations and practices; the increase in international tariffs and uncertainty over international trading conditions, changes in domestic and international economic and political conditions, the impact of the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, inflationary pressures, changes in interest rates, and others. These forward-looking statements speak only as to the date of this release and cannot be relied upon as a guide to future performance. authID expressly disclaims any obligation or undertaking to disseminate any updates or revisions to any forward-looking statements contained in this release to reflect any changes in its expectations with regard thereto or any change in events, conditions, or circumstances on which any statement is based. Non-GAAP Financial Information The Company provides certain non-GAAP financial measures in this statement. These non-GAAP key business indicators, which include Adjusted EBITDA, bARR and ARR should not be considered replacements for and should be read in conjunction with the GAAP financial measures. Management believes that Adjusted EBITDA, when viewed with our results under GAAP and the accompanying reconciliations, provides useful information about our period-over-period results. Adjusted EBITDA is presented because management believes it provides additional information with respect to the performance of our fundamental business activities and is also frequently used by securities analysts, investors, and other interested parties in the evaluation of comparable companies. We also rely on Adjusted EBITDA as a primary measure to review and assess the operating performance of our Company and our management. Adjusted EBITDA is a non-GAAP financial measure that represents GAAP net loss from continuing operations adjusted to exclude (1) interest expense, (2) interest income, (3) amortization, (4) stock-based compensation expense and certain other items management believes affect the comparability of operating results. Please see Table 1 below for a reconciliation of Adjusted EBITDA – continuing operations to net loss – continuing operations, the most directly comparable financial measure calculated and presented in accordance with GAAP. TABLE 1 Reconciliation of Loss from Continuing Operations to Adjusted EBITDA Continuing Operations. Three Months Ended March 31, 2026 2025 Loss from continuing operations $ (4,463,536 ) $ (4,339,467 ) Add back: Interest expense, net 2,428 12,712 Interest income (19,532 ) (51,544 ) Amortization 11,698 30,192 Stock compensation 1,040,058 454,339 Adjusted EBITDA continuing operations (Non-GAAP) (3,428,884 ) (3,893,768 ) Management believes that bARR and ARR, when viewed with our results under GAAP, provide useful information about the direction of future growth trends of the Company’s revenues. We also rely on bARR as one of several primary measures to review and assess the sales performance of our Company and our management team in connection with our executive compensation. The Company defines Booked Annual Recurring Revenue or bARR, as the amount of annual recurring revenue represented by the estimated amounts of annual recurring revenue we believe will be earned under contracted orders, looking out eighteen months from the date of signing of each customer contract. This estimate is comprised of two components (1) Committed Annual Recurring Revenue (cARR), which represents the minimum amounts that customers are contractually committed to pay each year over the life of the contract and (2) Usage Above Commitments (UAC), which represents our estimate of the rate of annual recurring revenue arising from actual usage of our services above the contractual minimums, that we believe the Customer will achieve after 18 months. The net amount of bARR reflects the deduction of the bARR of contracts previously included in reported bARR, which were subject to attrition, or other downward adjustments during the quarter. The Company defines Annual Recurring Revenue or ARR, as the amount of recurring revenue recognized during the last three months of the relevant period as determined in accordance with GAAP, multiplied by four. bARR may be distinguished from ARR, as bARR does not take specifically into account the time to implement any contract for authID’s services, nor for any ramp in adoption, or seasonality of usage of our biometric products but is based on the assumption that 18 months after signing these matters will have been generally resolved. Furthermore, bARR is based on estimates of future revenues under particular contracts, whereas ARR, whilst also forward-looking, is based on historical revenues recognized in accordance with GAAP during the relevant period. A reconciliation of bARR and ARR to a GAAP measure is not provided as there are no comparable GAAP measures and we believe that any attempt at such reconciliation may be confusing to investors. bARR and ARR have limitations as analytical tools, and you should not consider them in isolation from, or as a substitute for, analysis of our results as reported under GAAP. Some of these limitations are: bARR & ARR should not be considered as predictors of future revenues but only as indicators of the direction in which revenues may be trending. Actual revenue results in the future as determined in accordance with GAAP may be significantly different to the amounts indicated as bARR or ARR at any time. bARR and ARR are to be considered “forward-looking statements” and subject to the same risks, as other such statements (see note on “Forward-Looking Statements” above). authID INC. title: Organización de turnos y citas: estrategias para centros con varios especialistas
summary: ¿Tu centro de salud sufre por choques de horarios o salas ocupadas? Optimiza la agenda de tus especialistas, centraliza turnos y mejora la rentabilidad con estas estrategias de gestión clínica.
body_text: Gestionar un centro de salud no es tarea fácil, y cualquiera que haya vivido esa experiencia lo sabe. Coordinar la agenda de un equipo de especialistas no es lo mismo que gestionar la de un profesional independiente. Cuando hay varios profesionales compartiendo horarios, espacios y pacientes, la complejidad se multiplica y los errores tienen un costo mayor. La buena noticia es que con las herramientas correctas, todo eso se puede ordenar. Gestionar un centro con múltiples especialistas implica resolver desafíos que van mucho más allá de anotar citas en una planilla: hay que coordinar disponibilidades distintas, evitar que dos profesionales queden agendados en el mismo box al mismo tiempo, orientar rápidamente a los pacientes hacia el especialista correcto y tener visibilidad del estado de toda la agenda en un solo vistazo. Cuando eso no funciona bien, el impacto se siente en todos lados: en la experiencia del paciente, en el tiempo del equipo administrativo y en la rentabilidad del centro. Desafíos de la gestión clínica: ¿Cómo afecta el desorden de agenda a tu rentabilidad? Antes de hablar de soluciones, vale la pena nombrar los problemas que más aparecen en centros con múltiples profesionales ya que reconocerlos es también el primer paso para resolverlos. Sobreagendamiento de espacios físicos: cuando varios especialistas comparten box o salas de atención y cada uno gestiona su agenda de forma independiente, es frecuente que dos profesionales queden asignados al mismo espacio en el mismo horario. El resultado es desorden en la recepción, pacientes que esperan de más y un equipo que tiene que improvisar soluciones en el momento. Falta de visibilidad de la agenda general: si cada profesional maneja su propia agenda sin que haya una vista centralizada, la persona que administra no puede saber de un vistazo qué horarios están disponibles, qué especialista tiene espacio y cómo orientar rápidamente a un paciente que llama o llega sin cita. Disponibilidades que se pisan entre sí: cuando los horarios de atención de cada profesional no están bien definidos y separados, pueden generarse conflictos entre especialistas que comparten días o franjas horarias, o que trabajan en el centro solo ciertos días de la semana. Servicios mal organizados. Si los servicios de todos los especialistas conviven en una misma lista sin orden ni agrupación, tanto el equipo administrativo como los pacientes tienen dificultades para encontrar lo que buscan, lo que ralentiza el proceso de agendamiento y genera confusiones. Estrategias clave para organizar turnos y citas en centros con múltiples especialistas 1. Centralizar la vista de toda la agenda del equipo El primer paso para ordenar la gestión de un centro con varios profesionales es tener visibilidad completa de la agenda de todos en un mismo lugar. Sin eso, cualquier esfuerzo de coordinación se hace a ciegas. Esta centralización no sólo ahorra tiempo, también reduce errores y mejora la experiencia de quien llama o llega al centro buscando una hora. 2. Configurar salas de atención para evitar conflictos de espacio En centros donde varios especialistas comparten box o salas físicas, el sobreagendamiento de espacios es uno de los problemas más frecuentes y más difíciles de resolver manualmente. Al utilizar una plataforma digital como Encuadrado, puedes definir cada sala disponible, establecer su capacidad y asignar los servicios que se realizan en cada una. Una vez configuradas, el sistema bloquea automáticamente los horarios cuando un espacio ya está ocupado, impidiendo que se agende otro profesional o servicio en el mismo box al mismo tiempo. Esto elimina el riesgo de sobreagendamiento físico sin necesidad de coordinar manualmente entre profesionales. 3. Definir horarios de atención por especialista y por servicio Cuando los integrantes del equipo trabajan en horarios distintos, algunos solo ciertos días de la semana, otros en jornadas parciales, otros con disponibilidades que varían según el servicio que prestan, tener una sola configuración de horarios para todo el centro no funciona. Lo más eficiente es definir horarios de atención individuales por especialista y, cuando corresponda, por tipo de servicio. De esta forma, cada profesional tiene su propia disponibilidad reflejada con precisión, los pacientes solo pueden agendar en los horarios realmente disponibles y no se generan interferencias entre la agenda de un especialista y la de otro. 4. Agrupar los servicios por especialidad Un centro con múltiples especialistas suele ofrecer una variedad amplia de servicios. Si todos conviven en una misma lista sin organización, el proceso de agendamiento se vuelve lento y confuso, tanto para el equipo como para los pacientes que reservan online. Crea grupos de servicios por especialidad , de modo que cada profesional tenga su oferta bien ordenada y claramente diferenciada. Esto facilita la navegación para los pacientes, agiliza el trabajo del equipo administrativo al momento de agendar y da al centro una imagen más ordenada y profesional. Gestión manual versus software unificado: Comparativa de eficiencia para centros de salud Desafío Gestión manual Gestión con Encuadrado Coordinación de salas ✕ Alto riesgo de sobreagendarlar dos profesionales en el mismo box. ✓ Bloqueo automático de salas según disponibilidad y capacidad. Visibilidad de agenda ✕ Hay que revisar cada agenda por separado para encontrar un espacio libre. ✓ Vista global unificada de todos los especialistas en una sola pantalla. Autonomía del paciente ✕ El paciente debe llamar o escribir para consultar disponibilidad. ✓ Perfil online donde el paciente elige especialista, servicio y horario. Recordatorios ✕ Depende de que el administrativo envíe mensajes uno a uno. ✓ Automatizados vía email y WhatsApp para reducir inasistencias. Servicios y precios ✕ Listas largas y confusas que generan errores en el cobro. ✓ Servicios agrupados por especialidad con pagos integrados. Menos fricción para el equipo, mejor experiencia para los pacientes Cuando todas estas herramientas funcionan juntas, el efecto es inmediato y concreto. El equipo administrativo puede coordinar toda la agenda del centro desde un solo lugar, sin depender de comunicaciones entre profesionales para saber qué horarios están disponibles. Los especialistas trabajan con la tranquilidad de que su agenda está bien configurada y que no habrá choques de horario con sus colegas. Y los pacientes tienen una experiencia de agendamiento más clara y fluida, tanto si llaman al centro como si reservan por su cuenta desde su perfil.

Cosmic Rundown: Chrome's Silent AI, Async Rust Critique, and iOS 27 Wallet
summary: Google Chrome silently installs a 4GB AI model. Async Rust criticism resurfaces. iOS 27 lets users create their own Wallet passes. Plus Docker Compose in production, GitHub Actions outage, and the AI product graveyard.
body_text: Chrome Installs 4GB AI Model Without User Consent Google Chrome has been silently installing a 4GB AI model called Gemini Nano on user devices without explicit consent. The Hacker News discussion lit up with developers questioning Google's approach to user privacy and device storage. The model downloads happen in the background, consuming significant bandwidth and disk space. Users discovered it only after noticing unexplained storage usage. Google's position is that the feature improves on-device AI capabilities, but the lack of opt-in has frustrated developers who expect transparency about what software does to their machines. For teams building privacy-focused applications, this is a reminder that browser vendors make decisions affecting your users without your input. Progressive web apps and browser-based tools inherit these choices whether you want them or not. Async Rust Never Left MVP State A detailed critique argues that async Rust never matured past its minimum viable product state . The discussion draws nearly 200 comments from developers sharing their async Rust frustrations. The core argument: async Rust shipped with fundamental ergonomic problems that remain unsolved years later. Lifetime issues with async functions, the lack of async traits in stable Rust until recently, and the fragmented runtime ecosystem all contribute to a developer experience that feels unfinished. This matters for content platforms considering Rust for performance-critical backend services. The language delivers on speed promises but async patterns require more careful architecture than equivalent Go or Node.js code. iOS 27 Adds Custom Wallet Pass Creation Apple is adding a Create a Pass button to Apple Wallet in iOS 27, letting users generate passes from QR codes, barcodes, and tickets without developer involvement. The community reaction has been overwhelmingly positive. This changes the game for event organizers, small businesses, and anyone issuing tickets. Previously, creating Wallet passes required Apple Developer Program membership and technical implementation. Now users can scan any compatible code and save it directly. Content teams managing event ticketing or membership programs should pay attention. This feature democratizes a capability that previously required development resources. AI Didn't Delete Your Database A post titled AI didn't delete your database, you did confronts the growing trend of blaming AI tools for developer mistakes. The thread sparked debate about responsibility in AI-assisted development. The argument is straightforward: if you give an AI agent unrestricted database access and it drops tables, the failure is architectural, not artificial intelligence. Proper sandboxing, review workflows, and permission boundaries prevent these scenarios regardless of whether a human or AI executes the commands. This aligns with how Cosmic's AI agents are designed. Content operations happen within defined boundaries. Agents can create drafts and suggest edits, but destructive operations require human approval. Docker Compose in Production: The 2026 Take A practical guide asks whether you should run plain Docker Compose in production in 2026 . The discussion reveals that many production workloads still run on Docker Compose despite Kubernetes dominance. The answer depends on scale. Single-server deployments with reasonable uptime requirements work fine with Docker Compose and proper restart policies. Multi-node clusters with service discovery needs push toward orchestration platforms. For content-driven applications where CMS API calls constitute most of the workload, Docker Compose on a well-provisioned server often provides simpler operations than Kubernetes clusters. Quick Hits GitHub Actions Outage : A significant incident with GitHub Actions disrupted CI/CD pipelines. Teams dependent on GitHub's hosted runners experienced build delays and failures. Gemma 4 Multi-Token Prediction : Google released details on accelerating Gemma 4 inference using multi-token prediction drafters, promising faster local AI inference. Computer Use Cost Analysis : Research shows computer use agents cost 45x more than structured APIs for equivalent tasks, suggesting careful selection of when visual AI interfaces make sense. Instagram Encrypted Messaging Ends : Instagram's end-to-end encrypted messaging ends May 8 , forcing users to alternative platforms for private conversations. AI Product Graveyard : An AI Product Graveyard catalogs discontinued AI tools, serving as a sobering reminder of how quickly the AI product landscape shifts. What This Means for Content Teams Chrome's silent AI installation highlights browser vendors making choices that affect your users. Content delivery strategies should account for users who may have restricted Chrome features or switched browsers entirely. The async Rust discussion matters for teams evaluating backend technology. Performance gains come with ergonomic costs that affect development velocity. Apple's Wallet pass democratization opens opportunities for content teams to think about mobile-first ticket and membership experiences without custom app development. Cosmic's API provides the content infrastructure that works regardless of which browser, runtime, or mobile platform your audience uses. When the landscape shifts, your content stays accessible. title: Kelly named No. 2 on Forbes' 2026 lists of America's Best Temporary Staffing and Best Professional Recruiting Firms
summary: Kelly (Nasdaq: KELYA, KELYB), a global workforce strategy and solutions provider, has been named No. 2 on Forbes' 2026 lists of America's Best Temporary Staffing and Best Professional Recruiting Firms.
body_text: Rankings add to series of industry recognitions as company approaches its 80th anniversary TROY, Mich. (May 19, 2026) – Kelly (Nasdaq: KELYA, KELYB), a global workforce strategy and solutions provider, has been named No. 2 on Forbes' 2026 lists of America's Best Temporary Staffing and Best Professional Recruiting Firms. The rankings were announced by Forbes and Statista Inc. and are based on a survey of 13,800 participants composed of recruiters, HR managers, and job seekers. "These rankings reflect what Kelly does best: solving our clients’ most complex workforce challenges and connecting talented people to meaningful work," Kelly CEO Chris Layden said. "We meet critical workforce needs across specialized sectors like life sciences, engineering, technology, and education, and this recognition affirms that we are committed to ensuring every client and candidate we serve experiences the full strength of our expertise." The Forbes recognition comes at a time of strategic investments in people, technology, and capabilities as Kelly approaches its 80th anniversary in October. In 2026, Kelly strengthened the senior leadership team with key appointments focused on accelerating organic growth. The company is investing in a modernized technology stack, and its portfolio spans the full spectrum of AI-powered workforce solutions: Kelly connects more than 375,000 people with work every year and the company has been recognized for its industry-leading scale as the nation’s largest provider of education workforce solutions, the second largest engineering staffing firm, the fourth-largest life sciences staffing firm, and 11th largest technology staffing provider. In addition, KellyOCG consistently ranks among the top outsourcing and consulting firms, according to HRO Today and Everest Group. The company’s global workforce capabilities span staffing, business process outsourcing, managed service provider, and recruitment process outsourcing solutions to address clients’ total talent management needs, from filling single specialized roles to managing the full contingent and permanent workforce at enterprise scale. Kelly’s technology-enabled and AI-powered offerings keep people at the center, delivering a differentiated experience for clients and candidates, deeper workforce data and insights, and the speed and precision to match the right talent to the right opportunities. Earlier this year, Kelly was also recognized by Forbes as one of America’s Best Midsize Companies and one of America’s Best Employers for Company Culture . Kelly has also been featured on USA Today’s list of America’s Climate Leaders and Newsweek’s ranking of America’s Most Patriotic Companies . About Kelly® Kelly Services, Inc. (Nasdaq: KELYA, KELYB) helps companies recruit and manage skilled workers and helps job seekers find great work. Since inventing the staffing industry in 1946, we have become experts in the many industries and local and global markets we serve. With a network of suppliers and partners around the world, we connect approximately 375,000 people with work every year. Our suite of outsourcing and consulting services and solutions ensures companies have the people they need, when and where they are needed most. Headquartered in Troy, Michigan, we empower businesses and individuals to access limitless opportunities in industries such as science, engineering, technology, education, manufacturing, retail, finance, and energy. Revenue in 2025 was $4.3 billion. Learn more at kellyservices.com. # # # # Media Contact Christian Taske 248-561-8823 christian.taske@kellyservices.com

title: Global Payments Expands Partnership with Lightspeed DMS to Power Embedded Payments for Dealerships
summary: ATLANTA--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Global Payments Inc. (NYSE: GPN) today announced that its Integrated and Platforms business has secured the renewal…...
body_text: Investors News & Events Press Releases Press Releases Global Payments Expands Partnership with Lightspeed DMS to Power Embedded Payments for Dealerships May 08, 2026 8:30am EDT Download as PDF ATLANTA--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Global Payments Inc. (NYSE: GPN) today announced that its Integrated and Platforms business has secured the renewal and expansion of its partnership with Lightspeed DMS, a premier provider of integrated dealer management systems for the recreational industry. This new agreement exemplifies how the breadth of offerings from Global Payments enables growth for its partners as they look to expand their payments program and deliver innovative experiences to their customers. Since 2009, Lightspeed has partnered with Worldpay, now Global Payments, to provide payment and security services to its customer base. This relationship has been built on a consultative and collaborative approach, with Global Payments’ dedicated teams working closely with Lightspeed. As part of the next phase in Lightspeed’s payments journey, they will launch a new embedded payments offering. By employing Global Payments’ Payrix Pro technology, Lightspeed’s dealership customers will be able to manage payments directly within the Lightspeed platform as part of a more streamlined and integrated experience. The enhanced offering provides Lightspeed dealerships with greater visibility, control and efficiency within their daily workflows. “Global Payments’ commitment to partnership and dedication to drive continuous improvement have been instrumental in helping us serve our customers,” said Brian Provost, CEO at Lightspeed. “With this new embedded model, Global Payments has helped us grow at scale and deliver even greater value to our 4,500 plus customers that rely on Lightspeed to power their dealerships and drive their businesses forward.” Lightspeed will continue to rely on Global Payments’ commitment to operational and technical support to ensure seamless implementation. “Lightspeed’s trust in Global Payments for nearly two decades is a testament to the strength of our partnership and shared commitment to delivering value to their users,” said Matt Downs, president of Global Payments’ Integrated and Platforms business. “Through our strong partnership and alignment with Lightspeed’s executives, we are helping them execute a vision of providing their dealers with an improved experience for all things financial services. By delivering a platform that scales with their ambitions – so they can focus on innovation rather than building payments infrastructure – we are enabling Lightspeed to expand faster and with greater confidence. We are excited that Lightspeed chose to build their next generation offering on the Payrix Pro platform.” Lightspeed supports dealerships across the Powersports, Marine, RV, Trailer and Golf Car industries with a connected platform that helps manage sales, parts, service, rental, accounting, CRM and more. By expanding its partnership with Global Payments, Lightspeed is continuing to strengthen its platform with embedded solutions designed to simplify operations, improve the customer experience and support dealer growth. Global Payments completed its acquisition of Worldpay in January of 2026. About Global Payments Global Payments (NYSE: GPN) is a leading payment technology and software company that powers commerce for businesses of all sizes worldwide. We help businesses grow with confidence by delivering innovative solutions that enable seamless payment acceptance, smarter operations, and exceptional client experiences – online, in store and everywhere in between. With its global reach, local expertise and scale, Global Payments manages trillions in payments volume and billions of transactions across more than 175 countries. Headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia, Global Payments is a Fortune 500® company and a member of the S&P 500. Learn more at company.globalpayments.com . About Lightspeed Lightspeed is a leading cloud-based dealer management solution built for the Powersports, Marine, RV, Trailer, and Golf Car industries. Designed by dealers—for dealers—Lightspeed helps dealerships streamline sales, parts, service, rental, accounting, and CRM operations in one scalable platform. For over 40 years, Lightspeed has supported more than 4,500 dealers across North America with the tools and technology to grow their business, increase profitability, and deliver a better customer experience. Learn more at www.lightspeeddms.com . title: Build Replica Cars on an Open EV Platform
summary: An open, drive-by-wire EV skateboard built for replica and kit-car builders. Configurable wheelbase, SDK access, drivable on day one.
body_text: BUILD GUIDE 01 Why the Olympus EV Platform 02 A New Chassis for an Old Idea 03 The Hard Way vs. The Olympus Way 04 What "Open" Actually Means 05 One Platform. Every Wheelbase. 06 The Build, Without the Drivetrain Tax 07 Archetypes You Can Build 08 Specs & Pricing Explore the Platform The Olympus Skateboard is an open, modular EV platform built for the automotive industry — a revolutionary mobility platform for builders, entrepreneurs, and corporate R&D offices. We provide the chassis, the CAD, the schematics, the pin diagrams. You bring the body. The only thing left is your imagination. SECTION 01 Why the Olympus EV Platform The Olympus Skateboard is the result of a single decision: that the powertrain should not be the reason a vehicle program takes seven years. We built a complete, drivable, fully documented EV chassis and we sell it to the industry — to builders, to startups, to corporate R&D offices, to anyone with a body design and the conviction to put it on the road. The chassis is built with automotive-grade steel and is ready and waiting for the high-voltage and low-voltage elements to be assembled on top. Battery, motor, cooling, suspension, steering, brakes, cockpit electronics — already integrated and tested. We conduct every safety and hazard test in-house, so the platform you receive is a platform you can put your name on. Most EV platforms are sold to OEMs under NDA. The Olympus Kit is sold to you, with the manuals included. CAD designs. Electrical schematics. Pin diagrams. The full instructions, so a small team can move from sketch to driving prototype without reverse-engineering anything. 200 / yr Current annual production capacity, Irvine CA 2,000 / yr Target capacity by 2027 < 2 mo In-stock delivery window SECTION 02 A New Chassis for an Old Idea Replica building is one of the oldest acts of love in car culture. A builder studies a silhouette, sources a donor drivetrain, fabricates a tube frame, and spends two thousand hours putting it together in a garage. The result is something the factory never sold — a personal answer to a question the original car asked decades ago. The tradition is alive. The donor drivetrain is dying. Carbureted V8s are getting harder to source, harder to register, and harder to live with. Emissions law is closing in. The next generation of builders wants the silhouette without the apology. The Olympus Platform is the replacement for the donor car. A price that lands inside what serious builders already spend on a crate engine and a transmission — and a chassis that outperforms the donor in every measurable way. SECTION 03 The Hard Way vs. The Olympus Way Two paths to a finished replica. One assumes you are going to solve every problem in the powertrain stack yourself. The other assumes you would rather build a car. THE HARD WAY Without an open EV platform ✗ Hunt for a salvage carbureted V8 and a matching transmission. ✗ Fabricate a tube frame from scratch — measure, weld, jig. ✗ Build a wiring harness with no documentation. Reverse-engineer everything. ✗ Engineer a fuel system, cooling system, exhaust, emissions hardware. ✗ Spend 80% of the budget on powertrain before the body ever sees the chassis. ✗ Two thousand garage hours before the car will move under its own power. ✗ Then start the emissions paperwork. Approximate Cost $60K–$100K + ~2,000 garage hours, + emissions paperwork THE OLYMPUS WAY With the Olympus EV platform ✓ Skateboard arrives drivable. Battery, motor, suspension, brakes — integrated and tested. ✓ Chassis is built with automotive-grade steel. Safety and hazard tests already conducted. ✓ CAD designs, electrical schematics, and pin diagrams ship with the kit. ✓ Bluetooth and CAN exposed. Link your mobile app to the car and read vehicle data. ✓ Spend 100% of your time on the body, interior, stance — the parts builders actually care about. ✓ Mount the body on top. That is it. ✓ Electric — no emissions paperwork at all. All-in starting $27,500 Lite tier. Ships in under two months. THE DIFFERENCE YEARS → MONTHS · SIX FIGURES → FOUR SECTION 04 What "Open" Actually Means Open is not a marketing word here. It is a list of things you can do that closed platforms forbid. WHAT THE PLATFORM GIVES YOU >> Adjustable Wheelbase Length, width, height, and wheelbase configurable to your body. Shorter car? Shorter wheelbase. Truck? Truck-spec. >> Drive-by-Wire No steering column. No master cylinder. Clean sheet for the body. >> Bluetooth + Mobile SDK Bluetooth module included. Link your mobile app to the car and read live vehicle data straight from your phone. >> Low-Voltage Exposed Every low-voltage element is exposed and addressable — headlights, lighting, accessories. With pin diagrams. >> Olympus OS & SDK Write gauges, drive modes, telemetry. Tune throttle to the car you are building, not the one we shipped. >> Manuals Included CAD, schematics, pin diagrams, mounting hardpoints. Fabricate to spec, not to a guess. SECTION 05 One Platform. Every Wheelbase. Huge dimensional flexibility. Every dimension is configurable — wheelbase, length, width, ride height — dialed to the body you are building, not the body we picked. If you want to build a shorter car, we provide a shorter wheelbase. If you want to build an industrial truck, we provide a truck-spec wheelbase. According to your needs, your requirements, your build. Olympus EV Skateboard Kit v3.0 — automotive-grade steel chassis, ready for your body SECTION 06 The Build, Without the Drivetrain Tax The skateboard arrives drivable. Battery, motor, cooling, suspension, steering, brakes, and the cockpit electronics are already integrated and tested — every safety and hazard test conducted in-house before it ships. You spend your time on what builders actually care about: body, interior, stance, and the details that make the car yours. 01 Pick the Silhouette Sketch, scale, define wheelbase and overhangs. Decide the era and the shape you are answering. 02 Configure the Wheelbase Customized to your needs before the kit leaves the floor. We spec it to your dimensions. 03 Fabricate the Body Fiberglass, aluminum, carbon, hand-formed steel. The platform does not care. 04 Mount on Top Published hardpoints, documented CAN bus, real engineering drawings. Mount the body on the platform — that is it. 05 Tune & Drive Drive modes, regen, throttle map, dashboard. Then drive it. 06 Iterate Software-defined. Push updates, swap drive modes, tune the next car on the same chassis. SECTION 07 Archetypes You Can Build We are not in the business of telling you which car to recreate. We are in the business of making sure the chassis does not stop you. 01 60s Roadsters Aluminum-bodied two-seaters. Short wheelbase, big rear haunches, no roof. The archetype that defined open-top performance. 02 Race-Bred Coupes Le Mans silhouettes. Long, low, fastback. Built originally to win endurance races, now reborn without the fuel stops. 03 Mid-Engine Wedges The 70s supercar shape. Sharp creases, scissor or pop-up details, the silhouette that put posters on every bedroom wall. 04 Prewar Hot Rods Channeled bodies, exposed wheels, the American hot-rod silhouette. The platform's ground clearance and stance work in your favor. 05 Trial & Rally Replicas Boxy, light, mechanical-looking off-road archetypes. 19.3 inches of ground clearance does the rest. 06 Concept Cars That Never Shipped The drawings that died in design studios. Build the production version the manufacturer was too nervous to release. SECTION 08 Specs & Pricing A replica is judged in the first ten seconds of a drive.
